lines: In this episode, how the legal principles work in reality.
We look at how a court decides whether your use of force was reasonable, and proportional.

scenes.definition: A court puts itself into the victim's set of circumstances. Every situation is judged on its own specific circumstances.
lines: Now that we have established the legal principles, how do they work in reality?
Firstly, the test is not an armchair test.
A court will not assess the circumstances of the use of force without putting itself into the victim's set of circumstances.
This provides flexibility in determining whether your actions were legally justifiable.
Our courts acknowledge and accept that, in such a stressful situation, one cannot be expected to exercise the same degree of rational reasoning as one would had one not been in it.
Every situation must be judged on its own specific circumstances.

scenes.heading: Your belief must be reasonable
bullets: High crime: court more inclined to accept injury or death was probable
lines: Bearing in mind the high crime and violence levels in this country, it is probable that a court will be more inclined to accept that the probability of physical injury or death existed in a confrontation with a criminal.
However, your belief that you face a life threatening, or potentially life threatening, confrontation must be reasonable.
Your own subjective belief will not suffice to make your actions legally justifiable.
Your actions must be assessed objectively, by taking into account the specific circumstances in which you found yourself.

scenes.heading: Summary
bullets: Attacked, no time but to respond with appropriate force
If you reasonably believe there's a prospect of serious harm

lines.text: Simply put, say you are attacked, and you do not have time to do anything but respond with the appropriate degree of force.

lines: In other words, you don't have time to think about what your alternatives are.

lines.text: Your actions will then, in all probability, be legally justifiable.
As long as you reasonably believe that there is a prospect of serious harm to yourself, or somebody that you have a legal interest to protect.

scenes.definition: "Would a reasonable person, who faced the same or a similar situation to your own, have acted in the same or a similar manner in the same circumstances?"
lines: The test that the court applies is this.
Would a reasonable person, who faced the same or a similar situation to your own, have acted in the same or a similar manner in the same circumstances?
You should therefore only use your firearm for self or private defence if you are satisfied that your actions are reasonable.

rule.label: Remember
rule.text: Before using a firearm, be satisfied there is a reasonable prospect of serious physical injury or death to you or a third party.

lines: Furthermore, if you are going to use a firearm for self defence or private defence, you must be satisfied that there is a reasonable prospect of serious physical injury or death to you or a third party.
Only then will the law justify your killing somebody else in self defence or private defence.

scenes.heading: In conclusion
bullets: Use a firearm only after all other possibilities are exhausted
No time for other options: probably justifiable
Had other options, chose the firearm: may not be

lines.text: In conclusion, one should only use a firearm after all other possibilities have been exhausted.
If you do not have time to consider any possibilities other than the use of force or your firearm, your actions will probably be reasonably justifiable.

lines: They will be in accordance with the constitutional principles in this law section.

lines.text: Conversely, if you have other options, but you choose to use the firearm, then your actions may not be reasonably justifiable.

scenes.definition: Two considerations: the Excessive Use of Force, and the Intensity of the Force being used.
lines: There is one additional principle to consider when going into the mindset of self-defence.
This is the principle of Proportionality of Defence.
It covers two considerations: the excessive use of force, and the intensity of the force being used.

scenes.definition: Did the person defending themselves stop once the threat was neutralised, or continue beyond what was necessary?
lines: First, the excessive use of force.
Did the person defending themselves stop their defensive action once the threat was neutralised?
Or did they continue beyond what was necessary to neutralise the threat?

scenes.heading: The Intensity of the Force
bullets: Must match the intensity of the threat
Example: an argument escalates to a punch
A punch does not justify drawing a firearm
lines: Second, the intensity of the force.

lines.text: The intensity of the use of force must match the intensity of the threat that is being faced.
For example, a verbal argument between two men escalates into one of the men throwing a punch at the other.
That does not justify the second man drawing his firearm.

scenes.question: What test does the court apply to your use of force?
options: Would a reasonable person have acted the same way?
lines: Let's check what you've learned.

lines: One more.
A verbal argument between two men escalates, and one of them throws a punch.
Does that justify the second man drawing his firearm?
reveal: No. The intensity of the use of force must match the intensity of the threat being faced.
The book says a punch in an escalating argument does not justify the second man drawing his firearm.
